analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $15 an hour.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise the federal minimum wage to $15 an hour was introduced in January 2023, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act to raise the federal minimum wage from $7.25 an hour to $15 an hour, taking effect the first day of the third month after enactment. It was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, which never acted on it, and the Congress ended without any vote.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly millions of workers earning near the federal minimum of $7.25 an hour would see their pay rise, with the largest gains for low-wage workers in retail, food service, cleaning, and care work. Because the federal minimum has not increased since 2009, workers in states without their own higher minimum would gain the most.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage for regular employees from $7.25 to $15 an hour, effective the first day of the third month after enactment.
Because the federal minimum wage has stayed at $7.25 since 2009, the bill would deliver the first increase in well over a decade to workers in states that rely on the federal floor.

analysis.who_pays: Employers of low-wage workers would bear higher payroll costs, concentrated among retail, restaurants, hospitality, agriculture, and franchise businesses. Some of that cost could be passed to consumers through higher prices, and some employers might reduce hours or hiring. Low-income consumers would benefit from higher pay among workers.

drawbacks.text: Employers of minimum-wage workers would face roughly doubled wage costs on the federal floor, and small businesses and franchise operators in low-cost regions argue this could lead to reduced hours, hiring slowdowns, or automation.

The increase would be abrupt — effective about two months after enactment — with no phase-in period or regional cost-of-living adjustment, which economists across the spectrum note is a steeper jump than past phased increases.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would more than double the federal wage floor for the workers at the bottom of the pay scale, a substantial and direct gain for low-wage households. The cost falls on the businesses that employ them, and the abrupt, unphased timing makes the transition sharper than gradual approaches. On balance, the gains for workers earning $7.25 are large and concentrated, while the costs are spread across employers and consumers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never held a hearing or vote, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the Living Wage Now Act in the House on January 25, 2023.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
The bill attracted no cosponsors and no committee action; the full action history shows only introduction and referral.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that pay minimum-wage workers — restaurants, retailers, and franchise operators in particular — are better off because the bill died, as they avoid roughly doubled wage costs at the federal floor. Low-wage workers, who would have seen an immediate pay raise, gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Living Wage Now Act to raise the federal minimum wage to $15 an hour.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — for the entire two-year Congress.

against.name: House Republican majority (118th Congress)
against.role: Chamber majority controlling the committee calendar
against.what_they_did: Held House control during the 118th Congress and did not advance a minimum wage increase to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call positions were recorded; its sole sponsor and zero cosponsors signal very low bipartisan support, and the House majority that controlled the committee did not act on it.

industries.note: These industries employ a large share of minimum-wage workers and would bear the direct cost of doubling the federal wage floor. Their interest in blocking the bill ran against the workers who would have received the raise.
Workers earning near $7.25 an hour would have seen an immediate raise to $15, the first federal increase since 2009. This group includes many part-time, service, and care workers.
